prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art object detection and segmentation systems are fundamentally limited by the camera's field of view; they can only recognize visible surfaces. While "amodal" detection attempts to address partially occluded objects, there is a significant gap in detecting objects that are **entirely unobserved**—either because they are fully occluded by foreground elements or situated just outside the camera frustum. This limitation hinders autonomous agents (such as robots) from making intuitive inferences about their surroundings (e.g., inferring the presence of additional chairs around a partially visible dining table) which are critical for planning and active search.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that large-scale, pre-trained generative models (specifically Diffusion Models and Vision-Language Models) implicitly encode rich **spatio-semantic priors** regarding scene composition. We propose that these models can be repurposed to perform "passive inference." By treating the generation of unobserved scene regions as a variational inference problem, we believe we can recover a probability distribution of object locations. Essentially, if a generative model consistently "hallucinates" an object in a specific unobserved location based on context, that hallucination represents a statistically valid detection prediction.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a pipeline that predicts a **Spatio-Semantic Distribution (SSD)**—a conditional distribution over a bounded space mapping the likelihood of object presence given a single input image. We will investigate three generative strategies to estimate this distribution:

1.  **3D Diffusion-based Inference:**
    *   We will employ models capable of "Diffusion with Forward Models" to generate consistent 3D representations from a single RGB input.
    *   The system will render novel views (e.g., looking sideways or behind occlusions) from the generated 3D latent representation.
    *   Standard off-the-shelf object detectors will be run on these rendered "hallucinated" views.
    *   Detections will be back-projected into a common 3D voxel grid to accumulate confidence scores.

2.  **2D Diffusion Outpainting:**
    *   We will utilize 2D latent diffusion models to perform "outpainting," artificially expanding the image canvas beyond its original borders.
    *   Detectors will identify objects in these generated peripheral regions.
    *   For 3D localization, we will integrate monocular depth estimators to lift these 2D predictions into a 3D point cloud representation.

3.  **Vision-Language Model (VLM) Reasoning:**
    *   We will explore the reasoning capabilities of VLMs by querying them regarding spatial probabilities (e.g., asking the likelihood of an object existing to the left or right of the current view).

**Sampling Strategy:**
Crucially, strictly deterministic prediction is insufficient for unobserved regions. We will implement a sampling procedure where the generative process is repeated multiple times. By aggregating detections across these stochastic samples, we will build a normalized probability density function (a heatmap) representing where objects are most likely to exist, effectively quantifying the model's uncertainty.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **New Task Definition:** We aim to formalize the task of "Unobserved Object Detection" in 2D, 2.5D, and 3D settings.
2.  **Generative-to-Discriminative Bridge:** We expect to demonstrate that generative models can serve as effective priors for discriminative perception tasks, moving beyond image synthesis to scene understanding.
3.  **Robotic Utility:** Ideally, this approach will provide downstream probabilistic models for planning and navigation, allowing agents to make decisions based on what is *likely* there, rather than just what is strictly visible.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive framework to evaluate unobserved object detection across 2D, 2.5D, and 3D tasks. The following details constitute the technical configuration used to generate the reported data.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **RealEstate10k:** Indoor scene dataset. We filtered for scenes containing specific objects. We used 10 scenes from the test set. Images were resized to $360 \times 640$ for the expanded domain ($\mathbb{I}$) and center-cropped to $360 \times 360$ for the input image ($\mathcal{I}$). Average of 190 images per scene.
    *   **NYU Depth V2:** Indoor scene dataset. We used 10 scenes filtered by object frequency. Images were $480 \times 640$, center-cropped to $360 \times 640$ for the expanded domain ($\mathbb{I}$) and $360 \times 360$ for the input ($\mathcal{I}$). Average of 1359 images per scene.
    *   **Pre-processing:** We used one randomly selected frame per scene as the input image $\mathcal{I}$. COLMAP and GLOMAP were used for camera pose estimation and depth map reconstruction.

*   **Tasks Defined:**
    *   **2D Task:** Estimating the Spatio-Semantic Distribution (SSD) within the expanded image domain (pixel grid) from the input viewpoint.
    *   **2.5D Task:** Estimating the portion of the 3D SSD visible in the expanded image, centered at the input camera location.
    *   **3D Task:** Estimating the SSD over an expanded 3D region (voxel grid) accounting for out-of-frame detections and occlusions.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Normalized Cross-Entropy ($\mathcal{H}^{\times}$):** Measures alignment between ground-truth and predicted distributions. Lower is better.
    *   **Normalized Entropy ($\mathcal{H}$):** Measures the entropy of the predicted distribution.
    *   **Normalized Nearest Neighbor Distance ($\Delta$):** Quantifies spatial distance between peaks in thresholded ground truth and nearest peaks in thresholded predictions. Lower is better. Reported as a percentage.
    *   **False Negative Rate (FNR):** Classification error rate for thresholded detections. Lower is better.
    *   **2D Region-wise Accuracy ($\mathcal{A}$):** Coarse-grained classification accuracy over decomposed subdomains (left, center, right). Higher is better.

*   **Baselines & Models Compared:**
    *   **Uniform:** A baseline assigning equal probabilities across the grid.
    *   **Oracle:** A baseline with access to the ground truth realization.
    *   **DFM (Diffusion with Forward Models):** A 3D diffusion-based pipeline utilizing a transformer encoder with PixelNeRF and DDIM.
    *   **SDXL (Stable Diffusion XL):** A 2D diffusion-based pipeline using outpainting.
    *   **VLMs:** ChatGPT-4o, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Ultra, and LLaVa-v1.6-34b.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.
    *   **Object Detection:** YOLOv8x pre-trained on MS-COCO. Confidence threshold $\tau_{conf} = 0.1$.
    *   **Depth Estimation:** DepthAnythingv2 (for lifting 2D predictions to 3D).
    *   **DFM Settings:** Autoregressive sampling with 3 timesteps per frame, 50 intermediate frames. Temperature 0.85, guidance scale 2.0. Sampling took approx. 25 minutes per target pose.
    *   **SDXL Settings:** Diffusers library inpainting model. Input padded by 140 pixels left/right. Temperature 0.25. Prompt guidance scales $\{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$. Seeds $\{0, 42, 123, 999, 2021\}$. 10 prompts. Total 200 samples per scene.
    *   **VLM Settings:** Temperature 0.25, top-p 1.0. Queried 100 times per object/region/scene (total 6000 calls).
    *   **Evaluation Thresholds:** Classification threshold $\tau = 1.4 / |\mathcal{X}|$. Region-wise accuracy subdomains $\ell = 3$.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

The following observations summarize the non-numeric findings derived from the visual and textual analysis of our results and pipeline components:

*   **Observation 1 (3D Distributions):** We observed that the predicted 3D distribution domain extends beyond the camera frustum. Predictions indicated that the presence of occluded objects and out-of-frame objects (e.g., chairs around a table) can be inferred as likely, even when not directly visible.
*   **Observation 2 (DFM Pipeline):** The 3D diffusion pipeline demonstrated the capability to generate 3D representations from a single image. We found that aggregating samples from multiple rendered target camera poses ($k=4$) allowed for the recovery of occlusions in 3D.
*   **Observation 3 (2D Pipeline):** The 2D diffusion pipeline successfully expanded the image canvas via outpainting. Aggregating object detector confidence scores over multiple generated samples provided a viable 2D spatio-semantic distribution.
*   **Observation 4 (VLM Pipeline):** We observed that VLMs could provide coarse binary ("Yes"/"No") responses regarding object presence in extended regions (left/right). However, the spatial resolution was limited compared to diffusion-based methods.
*   **Observation 5 (Detection Capabilities):** In qualitative comparisons, the DFM-based model correctly inferred high likelihoods near ground-truth 3D locations for objects that were occluded (e.g., a sink behind a refrigerator) or out-of-frame. This contrasted with 2D methods which cannot model occlusion.
*   **Observation 6 (Failure Modes - General):** We observed performance degradation across all models for specific object categories, such as "door," which elicited frequent false negatives from the underlying object detector on synthetic images.
*   **Observation 7 (Failure Modes - Outpainting):** The SDXL outpainting model exhibited specific failure modes when not provided with object cues in the text prompt. In these cases, it often extended images with generic textures or unrelated imagery rather than the target scene context. Even with cues, we occasionally observed unnatural extensions that ignored the prompt.
*   **Observation 8 (Failure Modes - VLM):** In some failure cases, VLM-based models failed to report any detections where objects were plausibly present, effectively "missing" the unobserved objects entirely.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current object detection systems are fundamentally limited by the camera's field-of-view (FoV). While amodal perception techniques attempt to reason about partially occluded objects, they are unable to address objects that are entirely outside the camera frustum or fully occluded behind other surfaces. This limitation severely hinders autonomous systems, such as domestic robots, which require a semantic understanding of the unobserved environment for tasks like visual search, navigation, and adaptive planning. There is currently no framework that effectively infers the presence and location of objects that are not directly observed in an image but are likely to exist in the scene's vicinity based on contextual cues.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that large-scale pre-trained generative models (2D diffusion, 3D diffusion, and Vision-Language Models) contain sufficient implicit knowledge of scene composition and object co-occurrence to act as probabilistic priors for unobserved environments. By conditioning these models on a single observed RGB image, we can variationally infer a **Spatio-Semantic Distribution (SSD)**. We hypothesize that by aggregating multiple samples from these generative processes, we can recover a probability distribution representing the likelihood of specific object classes existing in the unobserved 2D and 3D space surrounding the camera.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework for **Unobserved Object Detection**. This framework will take a single RGB image $\mathcal{T}$ as input and predict a conditional distribution $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}}$ over a bounded space and a set of semantic labels.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Spatio-Semantic Distributions
We define the spatial domain $\mathcal{X}$ as the support of our target distribution. We aim to estimate the ground-truth conditional distribution $\Gamma_{\mathcal{T}}$. For each object label $o$, we will compute the SSD, denoted as $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}$. This function maps each location $x \in \mathcal{X}$ to a likelihood score:

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow [0, 1] $$

We will formalize this over two discretized domains:
1.  **2D Domain ($\mathbb{I}$):** A pixel grid extending the input image dimensions $H \times W$ to a larger canvas $H \times W^{\prime}$ (where $W^{\prime} > W$).
2.  **3D Domain ($\mathbb{V}$):** A voxel grid extending beyond the camera frustum, aligned with the input camera pose.

### 2. Generative Detection Pipelines
We will implement three distinct pipelines to estimate $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}$.

#### A. 3D Diffusion-based Pipeline (DFM)
We will utilize **Diffusion with Forward Models (DFM)** to generate 3D representations consistent with the input image.
1.  **Sampling:** We will generate a 3D representation conditioned on $\mathcal{T}$. From this representation, we will render RGBD images from a set of $k=4$ target camera poses (including the input pose).
2.  **Detection:** We will apply an off-the-shelf object detector (YOLOv8x) to these rendered frames to obtain 2D bounding boxes.
3.  **Back-projection:** The 2D boxes for object $o$ will be back-projected into 3D space using the rendered depth maps to form a point cloud of detection confidences.
4.  **Aggregation:** To approximate the distribution, we will repeat this generation process $n_s$ times.
5.  **Voxelization:** We will voxelize the aggregated 3D confidence map into grid cells $\mathbb{V}$. The final 3D distribution $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{3 \mathrm{D}}$ is obtained by averaging non-zero confidences per voxel and applying softmax normalization.

#### B. 2D Diffusion-based Pipeline (SDXL)
We will employ a latent diffusion model (SDXL) optimized for outpainting.
1.  **Expansion:** We will expand the canvas of the input image $\mathcal{T}$ (e.g., from $360 \times 360$ to $360 \times 640$) and use text-conditional generation to fill the unobserved regions to the left and right.
2.  **Sampling:** We will generate $n_s$ stochastic samples of the extended scene.
3.  **Distribution Estimation:** We will run the object detector on all samples to assign confidence scores for object $o$ to each pixel.
4.  **Normalization:** We will apply softmax normalization to compute the 2D SSD $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\mathrm{2 D}}$.
5.  **3D Lifting:** To estimate $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{3 D}}$, we will re-project the 2D detections using metric depth estimation (via DepthAnythingv2) and known camera parameters, followed by voxelization.

#### C. Vision-Language Model (VLM) Pipeline
We will adapt VLMs (e.g., ChatGPT-4o, LLaVa) for coarse spatial reasoning.
1.  **Input:** The model will receive the input image $\mathcal{T}$ padded with black pixels to represent the extended field of view.
2.  **Querying:** For each object $o$, we will query the model for a constrained binary response regarding the object's presence in the left, center, or right regions.
3.  **Confidence Generation:** We will aggregate responses over $n_s$ queries to produce a prediction confidence for each region, normalized to generate $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\mathrm{2 D}}$.

### 3. Evaluation Metrics Formulation
To rigorously evaluate the alignment between our predicted distribution $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}$ and the ground truth realization $\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{T} o}$, we will define the following asymmetric metrics.

**Normalized Entropy ($\mathcal{H}$) and Cross-Entropy ($\mathcal{H}^{\times}$):**
We define the entropy of the prediction and the cross-entropy with the ground truth as follows:

$$ \begin{array} { r l } & { \mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{T} o} : = \displaystyle \frac { - 1 } { \log | \mathcal{X} | } \sum _ { x \in \mathcal{X} } \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o} ( x ) \log \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o} ( x ) , } \\ & { \mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{T} o} ^ { \times } : = \displaystyle \frac { - 1 } { \log | \mathcal{X} | } \sum _ { x \in \mathcal{X} } \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{T} o} ( x ) \log \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o} ( x ) . } \end{array} $$

The normalization factor $\log | \mathcal{X} |$ ensures independence from grid resolution. This cross-entropy formulation specifically penalizes low likelihood predictions where objects exist in ground truth, but does not penalize high likelihood predictions in unobserved regions (accounting for the multimodal nature of unobserved scenes).

**Normalized Nearest Neighbor Distance ($\Delta$):**
We will quantify spatial accuracy by measuring the distance from peaks in the thresholded ground truth $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\tau}}$ to the nearest peaks in the thresholded prediction $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\tau}}$:

$$ \Delta_{\mathcal{T} o} : = \frac { 1 } { | \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\tau}} | } \sum _ { x \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\tau}} } \operatorname* { min } _ { x^{\prime} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T} o}^{\tau}} } \frac { \| x - x^{\prime} \| } { \mathsf { diam } ( \mathcal{X} ) } $$

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Novel Task Definition:** We will formally define the task of Unobserved Object Detection in 2D, 2.5D, and 3D, shifting the paradigm from visible perception to probabilistic spatial inference.
2.  **Generative Integration:** We will demonstrate how pre-trained generative models can serve as effective spatio-semantic priors for recovering occluded or out-of-frame objects without explicit supervised training on unobserved data.
3.  **Probabilistic Framework:** By recovering full spatio-semantic distributions rather than deterministic bounding boxes, this work will provide a theoretical basis for planning algorithms that must operate under perceptual uncertainty.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
